The Great eared nightjar (Lyncornis macrotis) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its evolutionary ecology as a tropical insectivorous bird. Neonates emerge from the incubating egg at a remarkably low body mass, with hatchlings weighing only 19.2 grams [Wwb = 19.2 grams] upon emergence. This modest initial mass is broadly consistent with the altricial developmental mode observed in many caprimulgiform birds, where chicks are brooded intensively and provisioned by both parents during the early nestling phase. The age at hatching, or incubation period, has been determined to be 35 days [ab = 35 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that is relatively protracted compared to smaller congeners and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the species' moderate egg size and the thermal demands of embryonic development in open nesting environments.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], several key developmental and physiological milestones have been quantified through field observations and captive rearing studies. Fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 33 days after hatching [tx = 33 days after hatching] at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This relatively early departure from the nest is typical of caprimulgids, which rely on cryptic plumage and immobility rather than extended parental brooding to evade predation. Subsequently, the attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is reached at 100 days after hatching [tp = 100 days after hatching], a developmental pace that permits individuals to enter the breeding population within the same calendar year in which they hatched, provided that environmental conditions and food availability are favorable at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C].

A detailed examination of reproductive output in Lyncornis macrotis reveals a conservative breeding strategy typical of many tropical aerial insectivores. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and field records consistently indicate that only one clutch is attempted annually [F_R_i = one clutch is attempted annually], even in regions with extended wet seasons. This low annual fecundity, amounting to just one offspring per year, is interpreted as an adaptation to a foraging niche characterized by unpredictable prey availability, where the energetic cost of producing and provisioning multiple broods would be prohibitive. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, derived from long-term banding studies conducted under active metabolic thermal conditions at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], is approximately 4855 days [am = approximately 4855 days], a longevity that is notably high for a bird of its body size and that underscores a slow life-history pace.

The ultimate adult body mass of Lyncornis macrotis exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature that likely influences reproductive roles and competitive dynamics during the breeding season. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 91 g [Wwi = 91 g], whereas adult males are substantially heavier, reaching an ultimate body mass of 105 g [Wwi = 105 g]. This size differential is reversed relative to the pattern observed in many caprimulgiform species where females are larger, suggesting that male-biased mass may confer advantages in territory defense or courtship display. In terms of metabolic physiology, the basal metabolic rate has been measured at 147.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 147.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when individuals are resting in their thermoneutral zone at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], representing the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded for this species.

The timing of first reproduction in Lyncornis macrotis is delayed relative to the onset of sexual maturity, a life-history phenomenon that reflects the challenges of territory establishment and pair formation in a long-lived species. The time since birth at first brood is 730 days [tR = 730 days], and this first successful breeding attempt typically occurs at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during active nocturnal foraging bouts. The deferral of breeding for nearly two full years after reaching puberty suggests that young birds require an extended period to acquire sufficient foraging skills, secure a breeding territory, and form stable pair bonds before attempting reproduction.
